name: Activated charcoal toothpaste

lead: Activated charcoal toothpaste is an over-the-counter dentifrice, sold as a paste or powder, that contains finely milled activated charcoal and is marketed for removing surface stains and whitening teeth. It became popular in the mid-to-late 2010s alongside a wider wellness trend and social media promotion.

Believers say the charcoal binds stains and gives fast, natural whitening. Published research is mostly laboratory work and a few small trials, and the American Dental Association has not given its Seal of Acceptance to any charcoal toothpaste.

paras: Two mechanisms are proposed: adsorption, in which the porous carbon is said to bind pigment molecules, and mild abrasion, in which the particles physically scrub extrinsic stains off enamel. Unlike peroxide products, it does not chemically bleach the tooth.

In-vitro studies report that charcoal products can roughen or abrade enamel and some dental restorations, and many products contain no fluoride. Dental organizations generally say the evidence for safety and efficacy is insufficient. The products are sold as cosmetics or toothpastes, not as approved drugs.

lead: Activated charcoal toothpaste is a category of over-the-counter dentifrice, sold as pastes and powders, that includes finely powdered activated charcoal as its headline ingredient and is marketed for removing extrinsic (surface) stains and whitening teeth [1]. Activated charcoal is carbon processed to be highly porous; the claimed actions are adsorption of stain particles and mild abrasion [1].

The products gained popularity in the mid-to-late 2010s, helped by celebrity wellness brands, influencer before-and-after posts and the striking black appearance of the paste [1]. In looksmaxxing and teeth-care discussions it is one of several 'natural' whitening routes alongside oil pulling and baking soda.

Published evidence is limited and largely laboratory-based. A 2023 systematic review of in-vitro studies assessed charcoal's whitening effect and abrasiveness [2], and later in-vitro work has examined its effects on enamel and on restorative materials [3][4][5]. The American Dental Association has not awarded its Seal of Acceptance to any activated charcoal toothpaste, according to a reference summary [1].
infobox: Activated charcoal, often with silica abrasives

paras: Activated charcoal is made by heating carbon-rich materials such as coconut shell, wood or bamboo and then activating the char with steam or gas to create a network of micropores [1]. The resulting black powder is milled and added to toothpastes or sold as a tooth powder [1].

Compared with conventional toothpastes, which typically use hydrated silica as the cleaning abrasive and include fluoride for cavity prevention, charcoal products make the carbon the key ingredient and many omit fluoride [1].

Charcoal toothpaste appears in forum discussions of teeth whitening as a low-cost, non-peroxide option. Compared with professional whitening or whitening strips, community posts often treat it as a lesser alternative.

A 2023 systematic review of in-vitro studies set out to evaluate charcoal's whitening effectiveness and abrasiveness [2]. A reference summary of that review reports that charcoal-based pastes generally whitened less than hydrogen-peroxide-based products and showed higher abrasive potential [1][2].
Because charcoal is not a bleaching agent, its effect is limited to surface stain removal, whereas peroxide products act on the colour of the tooth itself [1].

Laboratory studies have tested brushing with charcoal products on enamel, on composite resins and on CAD/CAM ceramic and hybrid restorations, examining roughness, gloss, colour and material loss [3][4][5][6]. Dental organizations summarised in secondary sources say that long-term use has been associated with enamel wear, sensitivity and rougher surfaces that may stain more readily, and that the evidence for safety is insufficient [1].
Because many charcoal products do not contain fluoride, and charcoal has been proposed to adsorb fluoride from other products, dental commentators have raised caries-prevention concerns [1].

A single-blind randomised controlled trial of 56 volunteers over 14 days compared activated charcoal powder, activated charcoal toothpaste, regular fluoridated toothpaste and 10 percent carbamide peroxide, measuring colour change, tooth sensitivity and satisfaction [7]. A separate randomised trial examined low-particle-size toothpastes against extrinsic stains [8]. Most other published work on charcoal toothpaste is in-vitro rather than clinical [2][3][5].

lore.intro: Charcoal toothpaste is discussed as a 'natural' whitening shortcut, with some users reporting visibly whiter teeth and others regarding it as a low-impact option compared with strips or professional whitening.

claims.claim: Charcoal adsorbs stains and whitens teeth quickly
Charcoal toothpaste is a safe natural alternative to bleaching

timeline.event: Celebrity wellness brands begin promoting charcoal products, helping bring activated charcoal into beauty and health markets [1].
Scientific and commercial interest in charcoal toothpaste peaks [1].
A systematic review of in-vitro studies assesses charcoal's whitening effect and abrasiveness [2].
